content_metadata.description: An educational video explaining the processes of transcription and translation of DNA, which lead to protein synthesis.

qAndA.question: What are the four ribose nucleotides involved in transcription?

qAndA.answer: The spliceosome enzyme cuts the pre-mRNA strand, removing sections called introns that are not expressed and keeping sections called exons that are expressed.
qAndA.question: What is the function of the spliceosome enzyme during transcription?

qAndA.answer: Three bases, known as a codon, code for one amino acid.
qAndA.question: How many bases on the mRNA strand code for one amino acid?

qAndA.answer: A codon is a sequence of three bases on the mRNA strand that codes for a specific amino acid. An anticodon is a sequence of three bases on a tRNA molecule that is complementary to a codon on the mRNA.
qAndA.question: What is the difference between a codon and an anticodon?

qAndA.answer: When the ribosome reaches the stop codon, the tRNA, mRNA strand, and the polypeptide chain of amino acids are separated, and the complex protein is released.
qAndA.question: What happens when the ribosome reaches the stop codon?

It is explained that three bases on the mRNA code for one amino acid.

It is explained that tRNA molecules have an anticodon on one end and an amino acid on the other.

As the ribosome moves along the mRNA strand, more tRNA molecules bind and more polypeptide bonds form.

The complex protein is released.

text_to_speech: Hi, this video explains how transcription and translation of DNA is important in protein synthesis. Protein synthesis is important in Biochemical engineering as they are used in bioreactors that make our food and medicines. So transcription, as the DNA strand unwinds, RNA polymerase causes the ribose nucleotides (A, C, G and U) to bind to their complimentary base pairings. As a result you get a single strand of RNA known as pre-mRNA. Then the pre-mRNA strand undergoes splicing where a spliceosome enzyme cuts the strand removing all the genes that are not expressed known as introns, keeping only the genes that are expressed known as exons. As a result a messenger RNA of exons exits the nucleus through its pores and attaches to a ribosome on the Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER). Translation, the ribosome binds to a start codon which consists of 3 bases that code for an amino acid. As the ribosome moves along the mRNA strand, translating RNA (tRNA) molecules with an anticodon on one end and an amino acid attached on the other end, bind to their complimentary codons. The 1st tRNA molecule binds to the mRNA strand, where the amino acid its holds binds to its neighbouring amino acid on the 2nd tRNA and so on. As more tRNA molecules bind to the mRNA strand, more amino acids form polypeptide bonds. As the ribosome reaches the stop codon; the tRNA, mRNA strand and the link of amino acids are separated. Finally, the polypeptide chain of amino acids folds into a more complex structure; hence a complex protein is released.
